passage:
'Nobody in this house gets it,' Pankaj said, dropping his bag.
Uma looked up from her laptop. 'Gets what?'
'Amma asked me to fetch vegetables. Today. When I had the worst day ever. She should know.'
'Did you tell her about the worst day?'
'She's my mother. She should just know.'
'Pankaj, she was on calls from nine to six.'
'And then Siddhu couldn't come to the ground either. Friends are supposed to be there.'
'Did you ask him?'
'I shouldn't have to ask.'
Uma closed the laptop. 'So everyone should read your mind, and when they can't, you're angry with them.'
Pankaj opened his mouth, then shut it.
'Tell me the worst day,' Uma said. 'I'm asking. Then you tell Amma at dinner.'
He sat down. 'Fine. It started with the bus.'

qa.q: How long was Amma on calls?
qa.a: Amma was on calls from nine to six.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj feel so angry that Amma asked him to fetch vegetables?
qa.a: Pankaj believes a mother should just know when her child has had a bad day, so an ordinary request feels like proof that she doesn't care.

qa.q: What turning point does Uma create, and what could Pankaj do with it?
qa.a: Uma asks to hear about the day, which shows that saying things out loud brings the understanding he wants; he could do the same with Amma at dinner and with Siddhu.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she learned Pankaj was angry about the vegetables?
qa.a: Amma would probably be surprised and sorry, since after a long day of calls she had no way of knowing about his worst day unless he told her.

grounding: Shows a teenager who expects his mother to know his mood unasked and a friend to always be free, and grows resentful before saying a word.

passage: Looking back at Class 11, I think I was angry with almost everyone. My parents should have understood that I hated science without me saying it. Lalremsiami, my best friend, should have been free every Saturday, because that's what best friends are. When she started badminton coaching on weekends, I didn't say anything. I just got colder. I left her messages on read. I told myself she should notice. She did notice, eventually, and asked me outside the library, 'Damini, what did I do?' And I realised I'd never actually told her anything. Not about the Saturdays, not about how lonely they had got. The resentment had grown for months; the conversation took ten minutes. We moved our plans to Sunday evenings. I still catch myself thinking 'should' about people. Now it's my cue to say something.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami ask 'what did I do?'
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked outside the library.

qa.q: Why did Damini get colder instead of speaking up?
qa.a: Damini believed a best friend should just notice and be free, so saying it out loud felt like it shouldn't be needed, and the hurt turned into resentment instead.

qa.q: What does Damini do now when a 'should' thought appears, and why does it help?
qa.a: Damini treats the 'should' as a cue to say something, which catches resentment early and gives the other person a real chance to respond.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami before that talk outside the library?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt confused and shut out, watching a friend turn cold without knowing why, which is why she finally asked straight out.

grounding: Shows someone looking back on a teenage year of expecting parents and a best friend to meet unspoken needs, and resenting them when they did not.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday
Gautam has seemed irritable all week, snapping at his group during the science project. Today he stayed back and let it out. His parents 'should understand' that he wants to switch to commerce; his friends 'should be there, every single time' for the project, and two of them went to a cousin's wedding instead. When I asked whether he had told his parents about commerce, he said, 'They should know. It's obvious.' He had not told them. He had not told his friends that the deadline worried him, either. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write three things he wished people knew, and next to each, one person he could tell. He wrote 'Papa' next to commerce. I've offered to be in the room if he wants, and I'll ask him on Monday how it went.
Nikita

qa.q: Which stream does Gautam want to switch to?
qa.a: Gautam wants to switch to commerce.

qa.q: Why does Gautam say 'They should know. It's obvious'?
qa.a: To Gautam the wish feels so clear that he believes his parents ought to see it without being told, so their silence feels unfair and feeds his irritation.

qa.q: What step did Nikita suggest, and why might it work?
qa.a: Nikita had him write three things he wished people knew and one person to tell each, which turns silent 'shoulds' into real conversations, starting with Papa.

qa.q: How might Gautam's project group see his snapping?
qa.a: The group may feel confused and hurt, since they had no idea the deadline worried him and only saw anger after two of them went to a family wedding.

grounding: Shows a teacher's note on a teenager who expects parents and friends to meet unspoken needs and grows resentful when they do not.

passage:
Friday

Papa booked the trip to Mussoorie for next weekend. The whole family. He didn't ask me. He SHOULD know I have the inter-school quiz finals that Sunday. I've been preparing for weeks. A good father would just know.

I didn't say anything at dinner. I just ate fast and left. Mummy asked if I was okay and I said "fine" in a voice that meant not fine. "Our son is sulking," she told Papa. She should have understood why.

Then I messaged Dolma to come over tomorrow and she said she has her cousin's engagement. Again. Best friends should be free when you need them. That's the whole point.

Now I'm lying here angry at everyone. Papa, Mummy, Dolma. Nobody even knows why.

...Which, okay, is maybe the problem. I didn't tell Papa about the date. I told Dolma nothing about why I needed her.

But they still should have known.

— Sahil

qa.q: What event does Sahil have on the Sunday of the trip?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz finals.

qa.q: Why does Sahil feel angry at everyone, even though nobody knows why?
qa.a: He believes his parents and Dolma should understand and be available without being told, so when they don't, he feels let down. The "should" rules make his resentment grow faster than any conversation.

qa.q: What turning point does Sahil almost reach, and what could he do next?
qa.a: He notices that he never told Papa the date or told Dolma why he needed her. Tomorrow he could tell Papa about the finals and tell Dolma what's going on, instead of waiting for them to guess.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he later learns about the quiz finals?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel surprised and sorry, wishing Sahil had told him before he booked. He might also feel hurt at being expected to guess.

grounding: A teenage boy believes his parents should know his plans and his friend should always be free, and his resentment grows faster than any conversation.

Tuesday. Jaya came home from tuition with a headache and three tests that week. Amma asked her to fetch vegetables from the corner shop. She should know I'm dying here, Jaya thought, and slammed the door on the way out. She didn't say a word about the tests.
Thursday. Jeevan texted that he couldn't come to the library on Saturday because of his cousin's engagement. A real friend would just be free, Jaya thought. She left him on seen.
Saturday. At lunch Appa asked why she'd been so moody all week. 'You should know!' she burst out. 'Nobody here notices anything!' Appa blinked. 'Notice what, kanna?' Jaya opened her mouth to explain and realised she had never actually told anyone about the three tests.

passage: Avni, you say we should just know when you're upset. I said the same at sixteen. Sit, let your Naveen Dadu tell you. That year I wanted to join the cricket camp in Pune. I never asked my father. I thought: if he loved me, he'd see how much I wanted it. Every evening I sat at dinner silent and sulking, waiting for him to notice. He didn't. My friend Ramu, who always came with me to the nets, started helping his uncle at the shop on Sundays. I thought a true friend should always be free, so I stopped speaking to him too. By the deadline I was angry at the whole world and had asked nobody for anything. My father found the camp form in my drawer after the date had passed. 'Why didn't you say?' he asked. I had spent two months angry at people for not reading a letter I never sent.

qa.q: What did Naveen want to join that year?
qa.a: He wanted to join the cricket camp in Pune.

qa.q: Why did Naveen sulk at dinner instead of asking?
qa.a: He felt resentful and hurt, believing that a loving father should see what he wanted without being told.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could have changed the outcome?
qa.a: Any evening before the deadline, simply showing his father the form and asking would have replaced two months of silent anger with a real answer.

qa.q: How might Ramu have felt when Naveen stopped speaking to him?
qa.a: Ramu was probably confused and hurt, since helping his uncle on Sundays had nothing to do with their friendship.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a teenager, he expected his father to understand without being told and his friend to always be free, and resentment replaced conversation.

passage: The power had gone out across the whole of Sector 9 an hour before Sangeeta's sixteenth birthday dinner, and the rain wasn't stopping. She sat on the balcony with a candle, checking her phone at twelve percent. Avni had texted at six: 'So sorry, Mumma won't let me cross the flyover in this rain. Tomorrow??' Sangeeta hadn't replied. A best friend would come anyway, she thought. Avni should just know how much tonight matters. And her parents should have known she wanted the rooftop restaurant, not dal at home in the dark; she'd hinted at it twice. Each thought made the next one hotter. By nine she had drafted a long message that began, 'I guess I know where I stand.' The phone died before she could send it. In the dark, the resentment had nowhere to go, and after a while it sounded a bit silly, even to her.

qa.q: Why couldn't Avni come to the birthday dinner?
qa.a: Avni texted that Mumma won't let Avni cross the flyover in this rain.

qa.q: Why did each thought make Sangeeta more resentful?
qa.a: She believed Avni and her parents should just know what she wanted, so every unmet 'should' felt like a betrayal, and the anger grew faster than any conversation.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do instead of sending the long message?
qa.a: She could tell Avni plainly she was disappointed and ask to celebrate tomorrow, and tell her parents directly what she had hoped for.

qa.q: How might Avni feel if that message had arrived?
qa.a: Avni would likely feel hurt and confused, having apologised and offered tomorrow, without knowing Sangeeta expected a visit anyway.

grounding: On a rainy birthday with the power out, a teenager thinks her friend and parents should know what she wants unasked, and resentment builds faster than talk.

passage:
Samir had been in a bad mood since Friday. Nobody seemed to notice, which made it worse. His parents should have seen he was upset about the football selection. He hadn't said anything, but they should have known. Instead Mummy asked if he'd finished his homework.

Then Sahil said he couldn't come cycling on Sunday; he had his cousin's engagement. He should always make time for me, Samir thought. I'd make time for him.

By Sunday evening a tight knot of resentment had built up. He didn't reply to Sahil's message: "bro wish you were at the engagement, food was amazing." At dinner he answered his parents in grunts.

Later Papa knocked. "Something's up, beta. We can tell you're upset, but we don't know what about. Can you tell us?"

Samir opened his mouth to say, "You should know," and stopped. They didn't know. He hadn't told them.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sahil come cycling on Sunday?
qa.a: Sahil had his cousin's engagement.

qa.q: Why did Samir feel resentful toward his parents and Sahil?
qa.a: Samir felt hurt and unseen, because he believed his parents should understand without being told and Sahil should always make time for him.

qa.q: What could Samir do instead of expecting others to know?
qa.a: Samir could tell his parents about the football selection and let Sahil know he missed him, so conversation can replace resentment.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa when he knocks?
qa.a: Papa is concerned and a bit confused, sensing that Samir is upset but not knowing why.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy who expects his parents to understand without being told and his friend to always be free, and grows resentful.

passage:
"You didn't come," Sarika said, arms folded, outside the chemistry lab.
Jasleen frowned. "To what?"
"My dance performance. Saturday. At the community hall."
"You never told me it was Saturday."
"You should have known. Real friends just know. Everyone knew."
"Sarika, I was at my Nani's in Amritsar all weekend. I didn't see any posts."
"You should always be there for the big things. I would be."
Jasleen's face went pink. "That's not fair. I'm not a mind reader. If you'd told me, I'd have come."
Sarika opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. She thought of her mother, too, who "should have known" she wanted her hair done at the salon and had plaited it herself. Sarika hadn't asked either of them.
"Okay," she muttered. "Maybe I should have told you."

qa.q: Where was Jasleen all weekend?
qa.a: Jasleen was at her Nani's in Amritsar.

qa.q: Why was Sarika so upset with Jasleen?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and let down, believing real friends should just know and always be there, so resentment built before any conversation.

qa.q: What could Sarika do differently for the next big event?
qa.a: Tell her friends and family clearly what she wants, and when, instead of expecting them to know.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel being blamed?
qa.a: Jasleen felt it was unfair and a little hurt, since she had never been told.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who expects friends and family to know what she wants without being told, and resents them when they don't.

passage:
I'm Joseph, and last year I spent my whole birthday week angry at everyone. My mother, Bhavna, should have known I wanted a small party with friends, not the usual family dinner. I'd dropped hints, sort of. And my friends should have kept the day free. Two of them had tuition. One went to a wedding.

I didn't say anything. I just got colder each day. When Amma asked what I wanted, I said, "Nothing," and then felt furious that nothing is what I got.

On the night, after the family dinner, I finally exploded: "Nobody in this house understands me!" Amma looked shocked. "Joseph, you said nothing. How could I understand?"

That sentence stuck. I'd built rules in my head, parents should read my mind, friends should drop everything for me, and then punished everyone for breaking rules they'd never heard of.

This year I told Amma what I wanted. We had the party.

qa.q: What did Joseph answer when Amma asked about birthday wishes?
qa.a: Joseph said, "Nothing."

qa.q: Why did Joseph grow colder each day of the birthday week?
qa.a: Joseph felt resentful and unseen, holding unspoken rules that parents should read minds and friends should drop everything.

qa.q: What changed this year, and why did it work?
qa.a: Joseph told Amma directly what was wanted, which turned hidden expectations into a plan they could share.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when Joseph exploded?
qa.a: Bhavna was shocked and probably hurt, having asked and been told "Nothing".

grounding: A teenager looks back on expecting a parent to read their mind and friends to always be free, and the resentment it built.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, by Chinmay
Sarita came to see me today, very angry. Her parents had booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday. "They should know it matters to me. I shouldn't have to tell them." I asked if she had told them. She said, "They should just know." Then she talked about her friends. Two of them couldn't come to her dance show last month. "Real friends make time for things like that. Always." She has been silent at home for three days.
I asked, "What happens when people don't do what they should?" She said, "I get angry and stop talking to them." "Does that get you what you want?" She was quiet.
What I did next: we practised one sentence she could say to her parents tonight: "This birthday matters to me. Can we talk about the dates?"

qa.q: What did Sarita's parents book?
qa.a: They booked a family trip for the same weekend as her friend's birthday.

qa.q: Why is Sarita so angry at her parents and friends?
qa.a: Sarita feels resentful because she believes they should understand and always be free without being told, and they fell short.

qa.q: What practical step did Chinmay offer?
qa.a: Chinmay helped Sarita practise one clear sentence to say to her parents tonight, so she could ask instead of expecting them to know.

qa.q: How might Sarita's parents see the three days of silence?
qa.a: They are probably confused and worried, not knowing that the birthday matters so much to her.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager who thinks parents should understand without being told and friends should always be free, and whose resentment grows faster than talk.

passage:
Saturday night
I'm so angry with Leela. I told her last week I had my first football match today. She should have known I'd want her there. Best friends should come without being asked. She went to her cousin's engagement instead. Didn't even message "good luck".
And Mummy. She should have known I'd be starving after the match. But she was at Nani's and there was only cold rice.
Everyone is always letting me down. Why do I have to spell everything out? People who care should just KNOW.
I haven't replied to Leela's "how was the match??" message. It's been four hours.
Actually, diary, reading this back, I never asked Leela to come. I said, "I have a match Saturday." That's not the same as "Please come." And I never told Mummy what time I'd be home.
Hmm. Maybe I'll reply to Leela.
Divyansh

qa.q: What did Divyansh tell Leela last week?
qa.a: Divyansh told Leela about the first football match on Saturday.

qa.q: What is Divyansh feeling about Leela and Mummy, and why?
qa.a: Divyansh feels resentful and let down, believing people who care should know what Divyansh needs without being told.

qa.q: What did Divyansh notice that could help next time?
qa.a: That saying "I have a match" is not the same as asking "Please come", so asking clearly could prevent the anger.

qa.q: How might Leela see the four hours of silence after her message?
qa.a: Leela might feel confused or worried, since she asked how the match went and got no reply.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows expecting a friend and a parent to understand needs without being told, and resentment building faster than conversation.

The week before Eid in Malerkotla, Farida sulked through every chore. Ammi should have known she wanted the green suit from the market, not the blue one Ammi had bought. She had looked at the green one for a long time, hadn't she? Ammi should have understood.
And Hafsa, her best friend since Class 1, should have been free on Tuesday to help with the mehendi, not at her aunt's. "She knew I was waiting," Farida muttered, though she had never actually asked.
By Chaand Raat she barely spoke to either of them. Ammi finally sat beside her with the blue suit. "Farida, what is wrong? Tell me in words."
Farida opened her mouth to say, "You should know," and then stopped. Did Ammi know? She had never said.

qa.a: The blue one.

qa.q: Why was Farida resentful towards Ammi and Hafsa?
qa.a: Farida felt hurt and resentful because she believed they should have known what she wanted without being told, and that "should" grew faster than any conversation.
